PUNITIVE DAMAGES AFTER THE REFORM ERA

INTRODUCTION

State legislatures have spent the last three decades narrowing the availability of punitive damages.[^1] This Article examines whether those reforms have achieved their stated goals.[^2] Part I surveys the legislative landscape. Part II turns to the empirical evidence. Part III proposes a framework for evaluating future reform efforts.

I. THE LEGISLATIVE LANDSCAPE

Roughly two-thirds of states have adopted some cap on punitive damages since the early 1990s. The caps vary considerably in structure.[^3] Commentators have long debated which structure better serves the deterrence rationale usually offered to justify punitive awards.[^4]

II. THE EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE

The empirical picture is more equivocal than reform advocates suggested at the time.[^5] Several studies find no significant relationship between damages caps and litigation rates.[^6]

III. A FRAMEWORK FOR FUTURE REFORM

This Part proposes that legislatures evaluate reform proposals against three criteria: administrability, deterrence, and compensation.[^7]

CONCLUSION

The reform era has not resolved the underlying tension between deterrence and predictability. Future legislative efforts should proceed with greater empirical humility.

IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE SEVENTH CIRCUIT

Marcus Whitfield, Appellant, v. Granger Industries, Inc., Appellee.

BRIEF OF APPELLANT

STATEMENT OF THE CASE

Appellant Marcus Whitfield worked as a machine operator at a Granger Industries plant for eleven years before his termination. He now appeals the district court's grant of summary judgment on his retaliation claim. This Court reviews a grant of summary judgment de novo. Baxter v. Cole, 1044 F.3d 900, 905 (7th Cir. 2015).

ARGUMENT

I. The District Court Applied the Wrong Standard.

The district court required Whitfield to produce direct evidence of retaliatory intent. That requirement conflicts with the burden-shifting framework this Court has repeatedly endorsed. Turner v. Vance, 12 F.4th 33, 40 (7th Cir. 2019). Under that framework, a plaintiff need only show that retaliation was a motivating factor. Ellis v. Moore, 500 F. Supp. 3d 12, 20 (N.D. Ill. 2021).

The company argues that Whitfield cannot satisfy even the relaxed standard. But cf Doe v. Farrow, 12 F.3d 88, 91 (3d Cir. 1994). That argument mistakes the summary judgment standard for the standard applicable at trial. The relevant statute confirms as much. See 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-3(a).

II. The Record Contains Sufficient Evidence of Pretext.

The timing of Whitfield's termination, coming eleven days after he filed an internal complaint, is itself probative of retaliatory intent. Baxter, 1044 F.3d at 907. The company's shifting explanations for the termination further support an inference of pretext. Turner, 12 F.4th at 42.

CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, this Court should reverse the judgment of the district court and remand for further proceedings consistent with this brief.
